Which ring goes where

One ring sits inside the lead circle, one outside, and the third switches from inside to outside once, between two leads.

Manufacturing rules and limits

Track cross-section

Off: each track is one width all the way round. On: a track carries less current towards its ends, so every segment between two leads is cut to I / (J × t) with J = the current-density limit above, never narrower than the sheet thickness (stamping web) and never wider than the track width, which becomes the maximum. Narrow segments make the two parallel paths less equal, which path balancing (below) can correct. Every segment is cut to the current-density limit except where the stamping web (≥ sheet thickness) or the room stops it; those segments run below the limit and are labelled on the plan. Plan, 3D, rules and the optimiser all use the stepped widths. Ticking the box shows the same design with the other section (it does not re-run the optimiser); the optimiser solves every sample both ways and the result tables say which one won.

Path balancing

On: a series resistance (about 75–150 mm of extra jumper wire) is added to the path that carries more current until both carry the same, never more than the bound in the rules above. Off (default): nothing is added and the optimiser balances with geometry only. The optimiser follows this switch and never turns it on by itself.
Without balancing, the imbalance is set by where the terminals sit on the open rings: the closer together the terminals must be, the higher it is. For this stator the best possible with terminals within 35° is about 3.4 %; allowing 60° gives about 3.0 %, 90° about 2.4 % (raise “Terminals within” in the rules and run again). Narrowing tracks cannot help: the sections only one path uses are already at the current-density limit.

The same 13 inputs the single-plane dataset run samples and logs, (ring arrangement, terminal order, thickness, both track widths, swap width, F-lead jog, both track shifts, plane raise, middle terminal angle and the two terminal gaps), with the run's ranges. Set from = to to fix an input. The rule limits above apply to every candidate.

Optimiser

Every rule, checked live

Standards used

DC link voltage is an input: set yours. 96 V is assumed. Insulation thickness follows IEC 60034-1 (test 2U + 1000 V) at 1/4 of the material's dielectric strength, with a moulding minimum wall.

How the dataset is made

1. A Latin hypercube spreads N points evenly over the unit cube, one axis per variable (each axis cut into N equal slices, one point per slice). 2. Each point is mapped to the ranges above (thickness to equal 0.25 mm levels, positions to a share of the free room, terminal gaps ≥ 10° with their sum ≤ the allowed span). 3. The design is built exactly as here and solved with the page's network. 4. Every rule is checked and its margin logged; nothing is rejected. Below: worker 1's samples, in order. Sample i is CSV row id 1000000 + i.

Conditions

A vs B vs C

A uses the values from the Busbar v7 Explorer at v7 defaults (20 °C, 360 A). B and C are solved here as a full resistance network with the geometry you set.
